questions.q: Identify the narrative point of view in "The Address" and name the protagonist.
questions.a: The story is told in first-person point of view ("I"); the protagonist is the unnamed narrator, Mrs. S's daughter. A wrong answer (e.g., "Mrs. Dorling" or "third person") reveals the student cannot distinguish narrator from other characters or identify narrative perspective — a basic comprehension gap that blocks all deeper analysis.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the narrator initially wants to visit 46 Marconi Street after the war.
questions.a: She feels curiosity about her mother's stored possessions and wants to see, touch, and remember the objects that linked her to her pre-war life. A wrong answer focusing only on "getting things back" or "confronting Mrs. Dorling" shows the student misses the emotional motive — the narrator seeks connection with memory, not material recovery — which is central to her character arc.

questions.q: The narrator says: "I was in a room I knew and did not know." Apply the concept of 'defamiliarization' to explain what this line reveals about her psychological state during the second visit.
questions.a: The line shows cognitive dissonance: the objects are familiar (she recognizes the Hanukkah candle-holder, the burn mark, the silver), but their arrangement in a strange, tasteless setting makes them feel alien. This reveals her trauma — the past cannot be reclaimed simply by physical proximity. A student who only paraphrases the literal meaning ("she recognized the room but it looked different") fails to analyze the psychological significance of the disconnect between memory and present reality.

questions.q: Compare the narrator's attitude toward the silver cutlery in the flashback (when her mother asks her to polish it) with her attitude during the second visit. What does this contrast reveal about her character development?
questions.a: In the flashback, she is bored and ignorant ("I didn't know the cutlery we ate off every day was silver"), taking heritage for granted. During the visit, she intensely notices the burn mark, the pattern, the gold border — showing heightened awareness born of loss. The contrast reveals her maturation: war and absence have taught her to value what she once overlooked, marking her transition from passive child to conscious survivor.

questions.q: Evaluate the narrator's decision to "forget the address" at the end. Is this an act of weakness (giving up) or strength (agency)? Defend your judgment with textual evidence.
questions.a: It is an act of strength and agency. She realizes the objects "lose their value when, severed from them, you see them again in strange surroundings" and that her current life ("a small rented room," "shreds of black-out paper") has no space for them. She actively *resolves* to forget — "Of all the things I had to forget, that would be the easiest." A student calling it "weakness" misreads her clear-eyed assessment of reality and her deliberate choice to prioritize present survival over past nostalgia.

questions.q: Create a diary entry (80-100 words) written by the narrator on the train back from her second visit, capturing her internal conflict and final resolution. Use first-person voice and include at least two specific textual details.
questions.a: A strong entry will show the shift from sensory overload ("the woollen table-cloth," "jingling of spoons," "muggy smell") to calm resolve ("I resolved to forget the address"), acknowledging the pain but affirming the decision. A weak entry merely recounts events without internal reflection, or has her regretting the decision, missing the story's thematic closure about moving forward.
